summary: This document presents considerations for link-layer addressing of Ethernet frames that carry MPLS-TP packets, in packet-switched transport networks.

plainLanguage.summary: When a package goes over an Ethernet link, someone must write the next stop's address on it. This explains how that is done for MPLS-TP.

questions: what multicast mac address does mpls-tp use
how do mpls-tp nodes learn the next hop mac address
what is the g-ach advertisement protocol ethernet interface parameters
subtitle: How MPLS-TP nodes with no IP find the right Ethernet destination address for the next hop.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP networks may have no IP, so ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery may not exist to learn the MAC address of the next-hop node on an Ethernet link.
tldr.mechanism: Use existing methods if present. Otherwise use a reserved multicast MAC address on links known to be point-to-point, or have peers advertise their unicast MAC address with the G-ACh Advertisement Protocol.
tldr.outcome: IANA allocated the multicast address 01-00-5E-90-00-00 and a new GAP application, Ethernet Interface Parameters (0x0001). Unicast discovery through GAP is the RECOMMENDED approach.

today: RFC 7213 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the GAP defined in RFC 7212.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is the set of MPLS protocol functions for building packet-switched transport networks. Since MPLS-TP packets are MPLS packets, the existing procedures for carrying MPLS over Ethernet (RFC 3032 and RFC 5332) apply.

What is missing is a way to pick the destination Ethernet MAC address. IP functionality is optional in an MPLS-TP network, so IP-based address learning such as ARP (RFC 826) and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) may not be available. This RFC specifies the options for choosing the next-hop MAC address when the nodes have no IP data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally computers ask each other 'what is your address?' using a tool that needs IP. These machines may not have IP, so they need another way to find out.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Link Addressing
sections.content:
If an existing mechanism can learn the peer's unicast MAC address, it SHOULD be used. Examples are ARP, Neighbor Discovery on an IP/MPLS network, or the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP). If none are available and both peers implement the procedures in Section 4, the GAP mechanism SHOULD be used.

The RFC then weighs the fallbacks. Static configuration of the peer's MAC address is an administrative burden, and replacing a faulty Ethernet interface means reconfiguring the peer, which is especially awkward when another provider runs the peer. The broadcast address FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF may cause excessive frame distribution and processing, and some devices treat broadcast specially.

If a non-negotiated address is to be used, both nodes should be configured to use an Ethernet multicast address reserved for MPLS-TP on point-to-point links. IANA allocated 01-00-5E-90-00-00. An implementation MUST default to passing MPLS packets received on a point-to-point Ethernet link with this destination address to the MPLS sub-system.

This only works when the link is known to be point-to-point. Otherwise broadcast or multicast addressing MUST NOT be used, so the implementation MUST let the operator declare a link point-to-point. Because a link supplied by an external provider may not stay point-to-point, declarations need care, and supporting the Section 4 procedures is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: If two machines share a private wire, they can write a special 'for my neighbor' address on every letter. That only works if the wire really has just two ends.

sections.title: Multipoint Link Addressing
sections.content:
When a multipoint Ethernet link serves as a section for a point-to-multipoint MPLS-TP LSP, and multicast destination MAC addressing is used, the procedures of RFC 5332 SHALL be used.

When a multipoint link (one not known to be point-to-point) serves as a section for a point-to-point LSP, unicast destination MAC addresses MUST be used. That means either static MAC configuration or a protocol that discovers the peer's MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: If many houses share one street, you cannot just shout 'neighbor'. You must write the exact name of the person you mean.

sections.title: The Ethernet Interface Parameters Objects
sections.content:
The G-ACh Advertisement Protocol (GAP, RFC 7212) lets a sender tell listeners on a link about its capabilities and configuration. On Ethernet, GAP messages are multicast to 01-00-5e-80-00-0d. Because GAP does not rely on IP, it can carry a node's unicast MAC address to peers without IP support.

This RFC defines a new GAP application, Ethernet Interface Parameters (0x0001), with two TLV objects:

  • Source MAC Address (type 0, length 8): an EUI-64 unicast MAC address of one of the sender's interfaces on this link, using the IEEE mapping from 48-bit MAC addresses to EUI-64 form.
  • Maximum Frame Size (type 1, length 4): a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order giving the maximum Ethernet frame size, in octets, that can be sent over the sending interface.

The MFS object MAY be used alone to advertise only the frame size where MAC learning happens by other means. If multiple advertisements are made for the same parameter, their use is undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: Each machine holds up a small card that says 'my name is this' and 'the biggest box I can take is this big'. Neighbors read the card and remember it.

sections.title: How the Discovery Behaves
sections.content:
Per RFC 7212, the information is retransmitted periodically and a receiver keeps it for the time given by the Lifetime field. To speed up link start, a node that was reconfigured, rebooted or knows it was disconnected from its peer is RECOMMENDED to send a GAP Ethernet Interface Parameters message and also a GAP Request for its peers' parameters at the earliest opportunity.

If the MAC address in a received Source MAC Address TLV changes, the new address MUST be used.

If a minimum MFS is configured for a link and the peer advertises less, the operator MUST be notified of the mismatch. The operator may then shut the link down, which triggers a fault and lets the end-to-end path be repaired, or leave it up and use an OAM message to verify the real MFS.

If the peer stops advertising, stops including the Source MAC Address TLV, or disconnects, the lifetime expires. After that the learned address MUST NOT be used, and the node returns to the method configured for the case where no advertisements are received.
sections.plainLanguage: The cards expire, like a milk carton. When a card gets too old, you stop trusting it and go back to your backup plan.

sections.title: Manageability
sections.content:
Values sent and received MUST be visible to operators, and when received information changes local configuration it MUST be clear why. The advertised Ethernet address and parameters for an interface SHOULD persist across restarts.

After a restart, any data kept from earlier Ethernet Interface Parameters advertisements from peers MUST be discarded, which prevents operating on stale data. If the link type changes, for example from point-to-point to point-to-multipoint, the operator SHOULD be informed, and if the new type is incompatible with the addressing method in use the system MUST take the configured action.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should be able to see what the machines learned and why they changed their minds. After a reboot, machines forget old notes so they do not act on out-of-date information.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Broadcast or multicast destination addresses can send MPLS-TP data frames to devices other than the intended nodes when the link is not point-to-point. Operators should make sure nodes know the link type. On multipoint links they should either keep unauthorized devices off the link or limit multicast delivery, for example by configuring the Ethernet switch to restrict multicast frames to authorized ports.

An attacker could disrupt communication by changing the Source MAC Address or MFS values. The RFC says this is mitigated by the cryptographic authentication described in RFC 7212. Seeing the TLV contents could help an attacker, and the RFC says this is best addressed by physical security of the links.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout a message on a busy street, strangers may hear it. And if someone swaps your name card for a fake one, letters go to the wrong place, so cards need a signature.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA made three changes. It allocated the Ethernet multicast address 01-00-5E-90-00-00 from the IANA Multicast 48-bit MAC Addresses block for MPLS-TP LSRs on point-to-point links. It allocated Application ID 0x0001, Ethernet Interface Parameters, in the G-ACh Advertisement Protocol Application Registry.

It also created the registry G-ACh Advertisement Protocol: Ethernet Interface Parameters, holding Source MAC Address (type 0) and Maximum Frame Size (type 1). The Type ID range is 0 to 255 and the allocation policy is IETF Review or IESG Approval.
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of official lists wrote down the special neighbor address and the two new kinds of name card so nobody reuses them.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Identifies the Source MAC Address object.

fields.name: MAC Address (EUI-64)
fields.desc: Unicast MAC address of the sending interface in EUI-64 form.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Identifies the Maximum Frame Size object.

fields.name: Maximum Frame Size
fields.desc: Largest Ethernet frame in octets that the sending interface can send.
